A mizer model with von Bertalanffy growth

Gustav Delius

Source: vignettes/von_bertalanffy.qmd

Introduction

The function newVonBertalanffyParams() builds a mizer model whose individuals, in the steady state of the model, grow along a prescribed von Bertalanffy growth curve. This is less immediate than it sounds. In mizer the growth of an individual is not a parameter but an emergent quantity: it is what is left of the assimilated food intake after paying for metabolism, and of that surplus only the part not diverted into reproduction contributes to somatic growth. To make this emergent growth reproduce a given von Bertalanffy curve we therefore have to choose the feeding, metabolic and reproductive terms with some care.

This vignette derives the construction from the ground up. We start from the von Bertalanffy curve itself, translate it into the energy budget that mizer uses, add reproduction, and finally deal with the awkward case of a negative von Bertalanffy age offset \(t_0\), where a naive implementation produces a discontinuity in the growth rate at maturity and where we show how to avoid it.

The von Bertalanffy parameters are supplied in the w_inf, k_vb and t0 columns of the species parameter data frame, together with the weight–length exponent b, the maturity weight w_mat and the maximum weight w_max.

Von Bertalanffy growth in length and weight

The von Bertalanffy model describes growth in length \(l\) by

\[ \frac{dl}{dt} = k_{vb}\,(L_\infty - l), \qquad l(t) = L_\infty\left(1 - e^{-k_{vb}(t - t_0)}\right), \tag{1}\]

where \(L_\infty\) is the asymptotic length, \(k_{vb}\) the growth rate constant and \(t_0\) the (hypothetical) age at which length is zero.

Mizer works in terms of weight \(w\), related to length by the allometric law \(w = a\,l^{b}\), so that the asymptotic weight is \(w_\infty = a\,L_\infty^{b}\). It is convenient to introduce the variable

\[ u = w^{1/b} = a^{1/b}\, l , \qquad u_\infty = w_\infty^{1/b} = a^{1/b}\, L_\infty , \]

which is simply length up to the constant factor \(a^{1/b}\). Because \(u\) is proportional to \(l\), it satisfies the same linear equation,

\[ \frac{du}{dt} = k_{vb}\,(u_\infty - u), \qquad u(t) = u_\infty\left(1 - e^{-k_{vb}(t - t_0)}\right). \tag{2}\]

Transforming back to weight with \(w = u^{b}\) and \(\frac{dw}{dt} = b\,u^{b-1}\frac{du}{dt}\), and using \(u^{b-1} = w^{\,1-1/b}\), gives the von Bertalanffy growth rate in weight,

\[ \frac{dw}{dt} = g_{vb}(w) = A\,w^{n} - B\,w \] where \[ n = 1 - \frac1b,\quad A = b\,k_{vb}\,w_\infty^{1/b},\quad B = b\,k_{vb}. \tag{3}\]

This is the growth rate returned by vonBertalanffyGrowth(). It is positive for \(w < w_\infty\) and vanishes at \(w = w_\infty\), where \(A\,w_\infty^{n} = B\,w_\infty\). The exponent relation \(n = 1 - 1/b\) is what ties the mizer growth exponent to the weight–length exponent \(b\).

The mizer energy budget

In mizer an individual of weight \(w\) encounters food at a rate \(E(w)\) and can ingest at most \(h\,w^{n}\) (the maximum intake). The fraction of the maximum that is actually realised is the feeding level \(f = E / (E + h\,w^{n})\), and the assimilated energy income is \(\alpha\,E\,(1 - f)\), where \(\alpha\) is the assimilation efficiency. After subtracting the metabolic loss rate \(\mathrm{metab}(w)\), the energy available for growth and reproduction is

\[ E_r(w) = \alpha\,E(w)\,\big(1 - f(w)\big) - \mathrm{metab}(w). \]

The construction removes every complication that would make \(E_r\) deviate from a pure power law:

  • Satiation is switched off by setting \(h = \infty\), so \(f = 0\) and the income is simply \(\alpha\,E(w)\).
  • Predation and resource interactions are switched off, so all of \(E(w)\) is an externally prescribed encounter rate rather than something that depends on the evolving spectrum.
  • The metabolic loss is linear, \(\mathrm{metab}(w) = B\,w\), obtained by setting the standard-metabolism coefficient to zero and the activity coefficient to \(k = b\,k_{vb} = B\).

With these choices we only have to fix the encounter rate so that the income is the power law \(\alpha\,E(w) = A\,w^{n}\), i.e.

\[ E(w) = \frac{A}{\alpha}\,w^{n}. \]

The energy available for growth and reproduction is then exactly the von Bertalanffy rate,

\[ E_r(w) = \alpha\,E(w) - \mathrm{metab}(w) = A\,w^{n} - B\,w = g_{vb}(w). \tag{4}\]

Before we account for reproduction, an individual therefore grows at precisely the von Bertalanffy rate.

External mortality

For completeness we note that the model also imposes a power-law external mortality \(\mu(w) = \mu_0\, w^{\,n-1}\), with the coefficient \(\mu_0\) chosen so that the steady-state juvenile biomass density \(w\,N(w)\) has a small negative slope (here \(-0.2\)). This gives a realistic steady-state size spectrum but does not influence the individual growth curve, which is our concern here, so we do not dwell on it.

Reproduction

Mizer does not put all of the surplus energy \(E_r\) into somatic growth. A size-dependent fraction \(\psi(w)\), the maturity ogive, is diverted into reproduction, so that the somatic growth rate is

\[ g(w) = \big(1 - \psi(w)\big)\,E_r(w), \tag{5}\]

and the remaining \(\psi(w)\,E_r(w)\) funds egg production. The ogive rises smoothly from \(0\) below the maturity weight \(w_{mat}\) towards \(1\) at the reproduction cut-off weight \(w_{\text{repro,max}}\). Above \(w_{mat}\) its switching factor has essentially saturated and

\[ \psi(w) \;\approx\; \left(\frac{w}{w_{\text{repro,max}}}\right)^{1-n} \qquad (w \gtrsim w_{mat}). \tag{6}\]

If we did nothing, Equation 5 would make the somatic growth \((1-\psi)\,g_{vb}\), which falls below the von Bertalanffy curve as soon as \(\psi > 0\). To keep the somatic growth on the von Bertalanffy curve we need the surplus energy to satisfy \((1-\psi)\,E_r = g_{vb}\), that is

\[ E_r(w) = \frac{g_{vb}(w)}{1 - \psi(w)}. \]

Since the unmodified budget Equation 4 already delivers \(E_r = g_{vb}\), we achieve this by reducing the metabolic loss by

\[ \Delta_{\text{repro}}(w) = \frac{g_{vb}(w)}{1-\psi(w)} - g_{vb}(w) = \frac{\psi(w)}{1-\psi(w)}\,g_{vb}(w). \tag{7}\]

The reduced energy spent on metabolism is exactly the energy that now flows into reproduction, so the total budget still balances.

It is worth checking that this reduction never exceeds the metabolic loss itself, which would make the metabolic rate negative. Setting \(w_{\text{repro,max}} = w_\infty\), so that \(\psi = (w/w_\infty)^{1-n} = u/u_\infty\) in the saturated regime, and writing \(g_{vb}\) in the variable \(u\) as \(g_{vb} = b\,k_{vb}\,u^{\,b-1}(u_\infty - u)\), we find

\[ \begin{split} \Delta_{\text{repro}} &= \frac{u/u_\infty}{1 - u/u_\infty}\; b\,k_{vb}\,u^{\,b-1}(u_\infty - u)\\ &= \frac{u}{u_\infty - u}\; b\,k_{vb}\,u^{\,b-1}(u_\infty - u)\\ &= b\,k_{vb}\,u^{b} = B\,w = \mathrm{metab}(w). \end{split} \tag{8}\]

This identity holds throughout the mature range where the ogive has saturated, \(\psi = (w/w_\infty)^{1-n}\): there the reproduction investment equals the entire metabolic loss, so the reduced metabolic rate is zero and the power-law income \(A\,w^{n}\) is shared between somatic growth \(g_{vb}\) and reproduction. In the maturation transition just above \(w_{mat}\) the ogive has not yet saturated, \(\psi\) is smaller, and the reduction is strictly less than \(B\,w\). Either way it never exceeds \(B\,w\), so the metabolic rate stays non-negative (and somatic growth stops only at \(w_\infty\), where \(g_{vb} = 0\)).

A negative age offset \(t_0\)

Everything so far assumed that a fish starting from the egg weight \(w_{min}\) at age \(0\) can follow the von Bertalanffy curve. This breaks down when the fitted \(t_0\) is negative. From Equation 1 the von Bertalanffy curve then places the fish at a positive size already at age zero,

\[ w(0) = w_\infty\left(1 - e^{k_{vb} t_0}\right)^{b} > w_{min}, \]

because \(e^{k_{vb} t_0} < 1\) when \(t_0 < 0\). A biological birth at a negative age makes no sense, and mizer must start every fish at the egg weight \(w_{min}\), which is far below \(w(0)\). The model simply cannot follow the von Bertalanffy curve over the whole juvenile range.

What we can ask for is that the fish reaches the maturity weight \(w_{mat}\) at the age the von Bertalanffy curve predicts, and that it grows along the von Bertalanffy curve from maturity onwards. Inverting Equation 2, the von Bertalanffy age at maturity is

\[ t_{mat} = t_0 - \frac{1}{k_{vb}}\log\!\left(1 - \frac{u_{mat}}{u_\infty}\right) = t_0 - \frac{1}{k_{vb}}\log\!\left(1 - \left(\frac{w_{mat}}{w_\infty}\right)^{1/b}\right), \tag{9}\]

with \(u_{mat} = w_{mat}^{1/b}\). A negative \(t_0\) makes \(t_{mat}\) smaller: the fish must reach maturity sooner than the plain von Bertalanffy rate would allow from \(w_{min}\). We therefore have to speed up growth below maturity.

The problem with a constant speed-up

The obvious way to speed up juvenile growth is to lower the metabolic loss below maturity by a constant factor \(c \in (0,1]\), replacing \(\mathrm{metab} = B\,w\) with \(c\,B\,w\) for \(w < w_{mat}\). The growth rate below maturity becomes \(A\,w^{n} - c\,B\,w\), which in the variable \(u\) is again a von Bertalanffy form,

\[ \frac{du}{dt} = c\,k_{vb}\left(\frac{u_\infty}{c} - u\right), \]

with rate \(c\,k_{vb}\) and a raised asymptote \(u_\infty/c\). Its age from \(w_{min}\) to \(w_{mat}\) has the closed form

\[ \mathrm{age}(c) = \frac{1}{c\,k_{vb}} \log\!\frac{u_\infty - c\,u_{min}}{u_\infty - c\,u_{mat}}, \]

which decreases as \(c\) decreases, so one can try to solve \(\mathrm{age}(c) = t_{mat}\) for \(c\). The fastest growth this can produce is at \(c = 0\) (no metabolic loss at all); if even that is too slow, one has to inject extra energy by raising the intake instead.

The trouble is that this speed-up is applied at full strength right up to \(w_{mat}\). At maturity the growth rate jumps from \(A\,w_{mat}^{n} - c\,B\,w_{mat}\) just below to the von Bertalanffy value \(A\,w_{mat}^{n} - B\,w_{mat}\) just above — a downward step of size \((1-c)\,B\,w_{mat}\). There is a second, subtler jump as well: if the reproduction compensation of Equation 7 is simply switched off below \(w_{mat}\), then, because the ogive \(\psi\) is already positive just below maturity, the somatic growth there carries an uncompensated factor \((1-\psi)\) and jumps by that factor at \(w_{mat}\). Either way the growth rate is discontinuous at maturity, which shows up as a kink in the growth curve.

Code
# Illustrative parameters (a mildly negative t0, so the constant-factor
# speed-up is feasible and its discontinuity can be shown cleanly).
b <- 3; k <- 0.38; w_inf <- 430; t0 <- -0.3; w_mat <- 69; w_min <- 1e-3
n <- 1 - 1 / b
A <- b * k * w_inf^(1 / b); B <- b * k
uf <- function(w) w^(1 / b)
u_inf <- uf(w_inf); u_mat <- uf(w_mat); u_min <- uf(w_min)

g_vb <- function(w) A * w^n - B * w
t_mat <- t0 - log(1 - u_mat / u_inf) / k

# constant-factor speed-up: solve for c
age_c <- function(c) log((u_inf - c * u_min) / (u_inf - c * u_mat)) / (c * k)
c_star <- uniroot(function(c) age_c(c) - t_mat, c(1e-8, 1))$root
g_const <- function(w) ifelse(w < w_mat, A * w^n - c_star * B * w, g_vb(w))

# tapering speed-up: Delta = s * w^n * (1 - (w / w_mat)^(1 - n)), solve for s.
# g_vb + Delta is again a von Bertalanffy form, so the age has a closed form.
Delta <- function(w, s) ifelse(w < w_mat, s * w^n * (1 - (w / w_mat)^(1 - n)), 0)
age_s <- function(s) {
    A_t <- A + s; B_t <- B + s / u_mat; k_t <- B_t / b   # modified vB coefficients
    log((A_t / B_t - u_min) / (A_t / B_t - u_mat)) / k_t
}
s_star <- uniroot(function(s) age_s(s) - t_mat, c(0, 1e5))$root
g_taper <- function(w) g_vb(w) + Delta(w, s_star)

w <- seq(w_min, 1.6 * w_mat, length.out = 600)
plot(w, g_vb(w), type = "l", col = "grey70", lwd = 6,
     xlab = "weight w", ylab = "growth rate dw/dt",
     ylim = c(0, max(g_const(w))))
lines(w, g_const(w), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(w, g_taper(w), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(v = w_mat, col = "grey40", lty = 3)
text(w_mat, 0, expression(w[mat]), pos = 4, col = "grey40")
legend("topleft", bty = "n",
       col = c("grey70", "firebrick", "steelblue"),
       lwd = c(6, 2, 2), lty = c(1, 2, 1),
       legend = c("von Bertalanffy", "constant speed-up (discontinuous)",
                  "tapering speed-up (continuous)"))

A tapering speed-up

The fix is to make the speed-up vanish at maturity so that the growth rate joins the von Bertalanffy curve continuously. Instead of a constant reduction we add a term \(\Delta(w)\) to the growth rate that tapers to zero at \(w_{mat}\):

\[ \Delta(w) = \begin{cases} s\,w^{n}\left(1 - \left(\dfrac{w}{w_{mat}}\right)^{1-n}\right), & w < w_{mat},\\[2ex] 0, & w \ge w_{mat}, \end{cases} \tag{10}\]

with a single amplitude \(s \ge 0\). The factor \(1 - (w/w_{mat})^{1-n}\) vanishes at \(w_{mat}\) and is positive below (since \(1 - n = 1/b > 0\)), so \(\Delta\) is non-negative and vanishes at maturity. The target somatic growth

\[ g_{\text{target}}(w) = g_{vb}(w) + \Delta(w) \tag{11}\]

is therefore continuous at maturity, equal to \(g_{vb}\) above it and faster below.

The reason for this particular shape is that \(\Delta\) is again of von Bertalanffy form. Expanding,

\[ \Delta(w) = s\,w^{n} - \frac{s}{u_{mat}}\,w = A_\Delta\,w^{n} + B_\Delta\,w, \qquad A_\Delta = s,\quad B_\Delta = -\frac{s}{u_{mat}}, \]

using \(w_{mat}^{-(1-n)} = w_{mat}^{\,n-1} = 1/u_{mat}\). Hence the below-maturity growth

\[ g_{\text{target}}(w) = (A + s)\,w^{n} - \Big(B + \tfrac{s}{u_{mat}}\Big)\,w = \tilde A\,w^{n} - \tilde B\,w \]

is itself a von Bertalanffy rate, with a faster growth constant \(\tilde k = \tilde B / b = k_{vb} + s/(b\,u_{mat})\) and a lower asymptote \(\tilde u_\infty = \tilde A/\tilde B \in (u_{mat}, u_\infty)\). Below maturity the fish thus grows along a von Bertalanffy curve that has been steepened just enough to reach \(w_{mat}\) on time, and which crosses the original curve exactly at \(w_{mat}\).

Because the below-maturity growth is a von Bertalanffy rate, the age to reach maturity has the same closed form as in Equation 2, and the amplitude \(s\) is fixed by requiring maturity at the von Bertalanffy age Equation 9:

\[ \mathrm{age}(s) = \frac{1}{\tilde k}\, \log\frac{\tilde u_\infty - u_{min}}{\tilde u_\infty - u_{mat}} = t_{mat}. \tag{12}\]

As \(s\) increases from \(0\), \(\tilde k\) grows and \(\tilde u_\infty\) falls towards \(u_{mat}\), so \(\mathrm{age}(s)\) decreases monotonically from the plain von Bertalanffy transit time at \(s = 0\) towards \(0\) as \(s \to \infty\). Any target age \(t_{mat} > 0\) is therefore reachable — unlike the constant-factor scheme, there is no lower bound on the attainable maturity age. Equation Equation 12 is a single closed-form expression, solved for \(s\) numerically.

Realising it in the energy budget

It remains to realise \(g_{\text{target}}\) within the mizer budget while keeping the reproduction compensation of Equation 7. Because the below-maturity target is itself a von Bertalanffy rate \(\tilde A\,w^{n} - \tilde B\,w\), we realise it in exactly the way the main curve was built in Equation 4 and Equation 7: the \(w^{n}\) term is carried by the (allometric) encounter income and the \(w\) term by the (linear) metabolic loss, with the reproduction investment again drawn from the metabolic loss. Writing

\[ \tilde A(w) = A + s\,\mathbb{1}[w < w_{mat}], \qquad \tilde B(w) = B + \frac{s}{u_{mat}}\,\mathbb{1}[w < w_{mat}], \]

so that \(\tilde A\,w^{n} - \tilde B\,w = g_{\text{target}}(w)\), we set

\[ E(w) = \frac{\tilde A(w)\,w^{n}}{\alpha}, \qquad \mathrm{metab}(w) = \tilde B(w)\,w \;-\; \frac{\psi(w)}{1-\psi(w)}\,g_{\text{target}}(w). \tag{13}\]

The subtracted term is the reproduction investment, generalising Equation 7 from \(g_{vb}\) to the target growth \(g_{\text{target}}\); it stays below \(\tilde B\,w\) (as in Equation 8), so the metabolic loss remains non-negative. One checks directly that \(\alpha E - \mathrm{metab} = g_{\text{target}}/(1-\psi)\), and hence, from Equation 5, the somatic growth is exactly \((1-\psi)\,g_{\text{target}}/(1-\psi) = g_{\text{target}}\), as intended.

This is the decomposition we want: the speed-up raises the encounter income through its \(w^{n}\) term (\(A \to A + s\)) and the metabolic loss through its \(w\) term (\(B \to B + s/u_{mat}\)), rather than being absorbed into a reduction of the metabolic loss. Consumption therefore stays allometric (\(\propto w^{n}\)) and respiration linear (\(\propto w\)) throughout. Below maturity, where \(\psi \approx 0\), this is simply \(\alpha E = (A+s)\,w^{n}\) and \(\mathrm{metab} = (B+s/u_{mat})\,w\).

The construction avoids both discontinuities of the previous section. The constant-factor jump is gone because \(\Delta\) tapers to zero at \(w_{mat}\); the reproduction jump is gone because the reproduction investment \(\tfrac{\psi}{1-\psi}g_{\text{target}}\) is applied continuously across maturity rather than switched off below it. The growth rate is therefore continuous. The encounter and metabolic rates individually step by \(s\,w_{mat}^{n}\) at \(w_{mat}\) — the coefficients \(\tilde A, \tilde B\) switch there — but these steps are equal and cancel in the growth rate \(\alpha E - \mathrm{metab}\), so they leave the growth curve smooth. Species with \(t_0 \ge 0\) have \(s = 0\), so \(\tilde A = A\), \(\tilde B = B\) and nothing about their construction changes.

Summary

The construction reproduces a von Bertalanffy growth curve in a mizer steady state by assigning each term of the energy budget a definite role:

Term Choice Purpose
Encounter \(E(w)\) \(\tilde A(w)\,w^{n}/\alpha\), with \(\tilde A = A + s\) below \(w_{mat}\) supplies the allometric income; carries the speed-up’s \(w^{n}\) term
Metabolic loss \(\tilde B(w)\,w\), with \(\tilde B = B + s/u_{mat}\) below \(w_{mat}\), minus the reproduction investment linear respiration; carries the speed-up’s \(w\) term and funds reproduction
Maturity ogive \(\psi\) mizer default with \(w_{\text{repro,max}} = w_\infty\) splits surplus into soma and reproduction
Speed-up \(\Delta(w)\) \(s\,w^{n}(1 - (w/w_{mat})^{1-n})\), \(s\) from Equation 12 corrects a negative \(t_0\) without a discontinuity

The result is a model whose steady-state somatic growth equals the von Bertalanffy rate above maturity, reaches maturity at the von Bertalanffy age even when \(t_0 < 0\), and has a growth rate that is continuous everywhere, including at the maturity weight.
